For the first time in so long, I felt a little bit of hope.

Maybe… maybe I don’t have to carry this pain alone.

It was hard for him to believe, but he did. He promised to help.

I refused, because I wanted peace, not drama. He agreed and never let me walk alone after that. He stopped smiling at Aisha the way he used to. He was with me.

It was still hard to walk past Aisha, but with Ishan, I felt safe.

I had two options, to heal or to suffer.

I chose to heal because I knew I didn’t deserve to suffer.

I chose to be in the drama club, to be seen, to be heard, as I deserved.

When I performed, I could see the spark of happiness in Ishan’s eyes.

A happiness I never thought I’d see in him again.

He was proud of me, maybe for performing in front of everyone, or maybe for surviving in this chaotic environment.

In high school, Ishan and I became something more than best friends, but we never named it.

Maybe we were afraid that giving it a name would change it.

That calling it “love” might break the spell.

So we kept it hidden, safe, unspoken, and ours. We started doing everything together.

Morning walks before school, shared bus rides, reading the same book and fighting over which character was better.

On Saturdays, we had a ritual,I’d bring cold coffee, he’d bring chips, and we’d lie under the tree near the abandoned library, talking about everything and nothing.

I once told him my biggest dream was to become a writer.

“Not a famous one,” I said, smiling up at the sky. “Just someone whose words feel like home to someone else.”

He laughed. “Then start writing, Wordsworth.”

“Shut up,” I giggled, tossing a chip at him. “I’ll write only if you promise to be the first person to read every word.”

“I promise,” he said. And I was happy at his word.

“Why do you keep writing about me so much?” he asked once, half-joking.

I looked at him, eyes soft.

“Because you’re the only part of my life that doesn’t feel heavy.”

That was the truth. He was the only place where I felt comfort, where I could just be.

Page 27 – High School

The months that followed were the golden hours of our story.

There was a winter trip organized by the school.

Everyone else was excited about snowball fights and selfies.

Ishan and I sneaked out early one morning before the others woke up.

The world was painted white, the trees bowed under snow, and our breaths curled like smoke in the cold air.

I stood in the middle of the road, arms wide, head tilted back, eyes closed.

“You know what this moment feels like?” I whispered.

“What?”

“Like time is holding its breath.”

And so was I, because all I could look at was him. I turned to him and smiled.

He didn’t say anything.

We had so much fun on that trip.

All the pain and suffering I had faced began to fade during those days, the laughter, the joy, the way he cared for me when I was on my period, it all made me fall for him even more.

We had grown up.

But when I looked at his face, I still saw the little Ishu, the same boy who once sat in class with wet socks.

He was such a pookie.

Page 28

After I came home from that trip, I had a lot of assignments to do, but he texted me:

“Look at the moon.”

He knew how much I loved the moon.

I quickly went to our spot, the place where we used to watch it together.

It was a happy time, and I felt so safe there.

I had always heard that perfect things don’t last long, and it turned out to be true.

I think that was the last time he and I shared joy like that.

Chapter 10

The letter trembled in my hands.

Every word echoed in my chest, like wind whispering her name through a hollow cave of memories. I read it once. Then again. And again. And still, it didn’t feel

real.

She had written about the trip, the silly photos, the roadside tea, the laughter, the quiet moments between songs. How she found peace in that escape. How that one

brief journey felt like breathing after drowning. And yet… that was it.

No word about what came after. Not a single syllable about the weight she had been carrying when we returned.

She’d left out the nights she stopped texting. The distant look in her eyes when we met by chance. The way her voice had grown smaller, quieter, like she was slowly trying to erase herself.

Why didn’t she write that? Why didn’t she write about the storm that swallowed her whole?

My fingers clenched around the paper, knuckles turning white. My chest tightened, not with anger, but with an ache so deep it made my bones feel like glass.

She was still smiling in those words. Still pretending.

And I… I had been too blind to see through it.

I let my head fall back against the cold wall of the bus. The road blurred past the window, a stream of grey and green. Somewhere in the distance, someone was laughing. That laugh felt like it belonged to a different world.

How could she carry so much alone? How could I have been so close, and missed it all?

I pressed the letter to my chest, as if holding it closer could rewind time, pull her back from the edge. But all I felt was paper. And absence.

“I’m sorry,” I whispered, voice cracking like glass. Sorry for being late.

Sorry for not noticing.

Sorry that your final chapter had no one to rewrite it.

I closed my eyes. All I saw was her smile from that trip.

And behind it… the silence she never spoke of.

A small slip of paper fell from the middle of the book. My eyes were drawn to the corner of the drawer, something tucked beneath a stack of old books and clothes.

A plain, worn-out diary. Brown leather, edges cracked. No name on the cover. No title. Just silence.

But my hands knew it belonged to her. I opened it.

And this time… it wasn’t poetry.

No carefully chosen words. No metaphors. No sugarcoated lines.

It was a war journal.

“I think my father stopped seeing me as a daughter the day I stopped obeying him like a puppet.” “My mother stopped asking me how I felt when she

started worrying about what the neighbors would say.”

“There were nights the screams in this house were louder than my thoughts. And I still pretended I was okay in school the next morning.”

Page after page. Truth after truth. Pain bleeding onto paper, not to be beautiful, but to survive.

She had written about holding her breath under her blanket at night, hoping her parents would stop fighting. About keeping her achievements to herself because they were never loud enough to be noticed in a home filled with anger. About birthdays that felt like burdens, heavy with broken promises and louder silences.

I didn’t realize it, but I had stopped breathing.

My fingers shook as I flipped through each confession. Each line a punch to the gut. She had lived in a warzone. And no one saw the wounds because she smiled too well.

I reached a page where her handwriting was messy, rushed:

“I wanted to tell you, Ishan. So many times. But how could I, when you used to talk about your happy family, your loving parents, your little jokes? I didn’t want to stain your world with mine.”

I shut the book suddenly, as if the pain might spill out and drown me.

I sat still for minutes that felt like lifetimes. Then I whispered, hoarse and hollow,

“I would’ve listened, Anya. I swear to God,

I would’ve stayed up all night. I would’ve burned down the whole world for you…”

But it was too late.

I wasn’t reading a cry for help. I was reading a eulogy written by the one who needed saving.

Tears blurred the ink.

But the pain? The pain was sharp. Clear. Unmistakably… hers.

And now, unbearably… mine too.

Chapter 11

I saw another diary, its cover still smelled faintly of fresh ink, its

pages crisp, as if they had only recently felt her hands. Unlike the others, this one wasn’t finished; the last page stopped mid-thought, mid-breath… as if life itself had interrupted her.

My heart sank. A part of me knew, no, I felt, that this was the one. The one where her words would finally give shape to the

darkness I had only sensed from a distance.

I sat there frozen, the weight of the moment pressing into my chest. My fingers trembled as I traced the edge of the paper, afraid to open it, yet unable to resist. Tears blurred my vision before I had read a single word. I wasn’t ready. I would never be ready.

I picked it up with both hands, as if it were made of glass.

It was heavier than anything I had ever held, not because of its size, but because I knew.

I knew that whatever lived inside these pages would change me. Would break me.

I stared at it for what felt like forever. The room didn’t move. Neither did I. Just the diary… and my heart, beating in uneven bursts.

Slowly, I turned it over, half-expecting a lock, a name, something to prepare me.

Nothing.

Only that feather.

I opened the first page. Blank. Second page. Blank.

And then…

“To whoever finds this—

Don’t read this unless you’re ready to break. This isn’t a story.

It’s a scream I couldn’t let out loud.

And if you’re reading it… I’m probably gone.

But maybe, just maybe, you’ll understand me now.”

— Anya

I swallowed hard. The lump in my throat refused to go away.

The words swam in front of me, blurred by the tears filling my eyes, but I didn’t wipe them this time. She had written this knowing someone would find it. Hoping they would.

I wasn’t ready. But I had to be.

My fingers, unsteady, turned the page. The first entry stared back at me. Dated six months ago.

I didn’t read it. Not yet. Something in me wasn’t ready to step inside the world she had kept locked away.

Instead, I clutched the diary to my chest like a lifeline. Like it was all I had left of her now.

Outside, the rain began to slow. Inside, my world was only just beginning to fall apart.

The night we came back from the trip, I remember tilting my head back and staring at the sky. The moon hung there, impossibly bright—fuller than I’d ever seen it. It was the kind of glow that makes you think someone painted it just for you, like the universe was trying to whisper: hold on a little longer.

I stood on our rooftop, the night air clinging to my skin, my shawl wrapped tight around me.

For a moment, I let myself believe. Believe that maybe… just maybe… things could turn around. That maybe I was still allowed to hope.

I didn’t know it then, but that was the last peaceful night I would ever have.

Chapter 12

The night before, the moon had told me to

hope.

By the next evening, hope had already started packing its bags.

I remember the exact day. The day the ground shifted.

The day my father stopped being Baba and became a man I didn’t recognize.

It was a Wednesday.

I know because I had chemistry practical that morning, and I was excited to tell him I finally got the titration right, after weeks of messing it up. I had even kept the lab coat folded neatly, thinking he’d be proud.

When I stepped into the house, the air felt wrong. The curtains were drawn, unusual for noon, and there was this thick silence hanging in the living room, like something ugly had just happened.

And then I saw it.

Dad’s phone lay shattered on the floor, next to the

glass tea table that was now split in two. Tea seeped into the rug like blood, and Mom stood in the corner, arms crossed over her chest, eyes red, not crying, just blinking, like she was trying to rewind time.

He looked at me like I shouldn’t be there. And I should’ve left. But I didn’t.

“Baba?” I whispered.

He didn’t answer. Just walked past me into the study and slammed the door so hard the painting on the hallway wall tilted sideways.

I went to Mom.

She just said, “It’s finished. Everything’s gone.”

I didn’t understand. Not fully.

Later that night, I found out, Dad’s partner had backed out of a crucial deal. Years of paperwork, investments, sleepless nights… all for nothing. The company he built from the ground up, the one he always talked about like it was his firstborn, had crumbled.

And along with it, so did he.

But not like a man grieving.

Like a man angry at the world for watching him fall.

He became colder. His voice, louder.

His hands, not violent, but never gentle again.

That same night, I walked into the dining room, and he was sitting there, staring at the TV, not watching. The light from the screen cast a dull blue over his face. He looked like a stranger.

I gently placed my lab coat on the table.

“I topped the chemistry practical today,” I said, softly.

He didn’t move.

I tried again. “Thought you’d be proud.” He looked at me then.

And what he said broke something inside me I never fixed.

“You think your marks matter right now? Do you know what it feels like to lose everything? Or do you just float around in your little world, writing poems and wasting my money on notebooks?”

I froze.

Not because of what he said — but because of how he said it.

Like I was the mistake he couldn’t afford anymore.

After that night, he barely spoke to me. If he did, it was clipped, cold, transactional.

Sometimes I heard him cry in the bathroom. Sometimes I heard him shout at Mom for coughing too loudly.

But mostly, he just sat in silence, defeated, bitter, and ashamed.

I started walking on eggshells. Timed my entries and exits.

Lowered my voice. Stopped playing music.

Stopped laughing too loudly. Stopped being… me.

Every day I came home, I waited for another outburst, even if it never came.

That’s the thing about trauma… it makes silence terrifying too.

I still have that cracked lab coat.

It’s folded in the back of my cupboard, stained with

a drop of tea from that day. I never washed it.

I don’t know why.

Maybe because it reminds me of the last time I tried to make him proud.

Maybe because that was the last day I was still his daughter.

Or maybe… because some stains aren’t meant to be cleaned.

It didn’t happen all at once.

Not like in the movies, where someone faints or screams or clutches their chest.

My mother… she disappeared quietly.

At first, I thought she was just tired.

After all, everything was falling apart, Dad’s business, their marriage, our home.

Tiredness seemed normal. But this was something else.

She stopped dressing properly. Stopped humming songs while cooking.

Stopped correcting my posture at the dining table.

She’d just sit in the corner of the sofa, arms wrapped tight around herself like she was trying to keep her body from spilling apart.

Her eyes would drift toward nothing, blank, as if her mind was elsewhere… or nowhere.

The first time I truly noticed it was the night I found her on the kitchen floor at 3 a.m.

I had woken up for water. The lights were on. I thought maybe she’d left the gas on by mistake.

But when I stepped in, she was sitting there, back against the lower cabinet, tears sliding down her cheeks in complete silence.

No sobbing.

Just leaking, like she’d forgotten how to stop. “Mom?” I whispered.

She looked up at me, startled, almost ashamed to be seen.

“I was just… I thought I left the stove on,” she murmured.

There was no stove. Just her.

And an empty cup in her hand that she must’ve been holding for hours.

I helped her back to bed. Her hands were cold.

Her breathing was shallow. She looked so small.

So defeated.

That’s when I knew, something inside her was breaking.

After that, it got worse.

She started forgetting things, the day of the week, whether she’d eaten, sometimes even my name. Once she tried to make tea and boiled rice instead. She stared at it for five minutes, as if it might change.

She began avoiding sunlight. Closed all the windows.

The house smelled like sadness, stale, heavy, unmoving.

We took her to a doctor.

They said it could be depression, maybe cognitive fatigue.

Prescribed medication. Routine. Rest.

But how do you give rest to a heart that’s been breaking for years?

Dad said nothing during the appointment.

When we got home, he yelled, called her “dramatic”

and “weak,” accused her of “ruining what little peace we had left.”

She didn’t fight back.

She just nodded like a guilty child, swallowed her pills, and went back to bed with the curtains drawn.

And I?

I was seventeen.

Not old enough to save her.

Not strong enough to carry two broken parents on my back.

But I tried.

I cooked. Cleaned. Paid the electricity bill when Dad forgot. Walked to the pharmacy alone for her antidepressants.

Sometimes, I even sang to her, old Nepali songs she used to hum before bedtime when I was little. She would smile faintly.

But her eyes… they were always far away.

Like she was living in a memory where she was still young, still in love, still happy.

Somewhere I couldn’t reach.

The worst part?

She never spoke about it.

Never cried in front of me again. Never admitted she was unwell.

She just faded, a little more every day, like the ink on old letters.

And I kept watching, helpless, as the woman who once braided my hair and tucked me into bed… slowly became a stranger in her own body.

One day, I caught her staring at the ceiling and whispering.

I leaned in.

She was saying my name. Again and again.

But not like a prayer. Like a goodbye.

Chapter 13

I started avoiding Ishan the day my father broke the tea

table.

Not because I stopped caring.

But because everything changed after that crash.

He had screamed loud enough to wake the whole neighborhood.

Called me useless.

Shoved my books off the table because I forgot to make him tea.

Slammed the door so hard a photo of us, happy, years old, fell and cracked.

I didn’t go to class the next day. I couldn’t.

My hands were still trembling. My cheek still burned from the words, not his palm.

Ishan texted, like always.

Did you oversleep again? Want me to bring notes?

I typed, No. Just tired.

Then deleted it.

Because he would ask. He always did.

And I couldn’t let him see the mess I was becoming, the mess I was born into.

Then came my mother’s collapse.

It started small, forgetting things, whispering to herself, sleeping more than she was awake.

But one day she dropped a plate, sank to the floor, and began crying like a lost child.

“I can’t feel anything anymore,” she said.

That night I stayed beside her bed, listening to her shiver and cry in her sleep.

Ishan called around midnight.

His name lit up my screen, Ishu calling...

I didn’t answer.

If he heard my voice, he’d know. And I’d fall apart.

He was preparing for entrance exams. Scholarships. A life.

My brokenness didn’t belong in his future. So I let the phone ring until it died.

He started to worry.

His messages became less playful, more urgent.

I know something’s wrong. Please talk to me. Anya, I’m here. Don’t shut me out.

Don’t do this. Not like this.

Each one was a knife.

But I thought I was protecting him.

While he rose, late-night study sessions, career goals, future cities, I sat beside a mother who barely knew her own name, and a father who treated silence like punishment.

Then came my birthday.

He remembered. He always did.

Even when we were kids, he’d draw handmade cards, crooked stars, lopsided cupcakes.

A week before, he’d messaged: This year, you’re not escaping. I’m planning something.

The day before: Don’t make me wait alone. Just one hour, Anya.

That day, Mom locked herself in the bathroom again.

I spent the afternoon whispering poems through the door until she came out.

By the time I looked at the clock, it was four, the time I was supposed to meet him.

I turned my phone off.

And cried against the kitchen wall.

He waited. I know he did. But this time… he stopped.

After that, weeks passed. Then months.

He got a part-time job. Went to class on time. Dressed better. Smiled more, not like before, but enough.

He was moving forward. Without me.

We still sent quick texts:

How are things? Okay. You?

Busy. Just working.

We both paused, every time, waiting for I miss you.

Neither of us said it.

Love had become too fragile to touch.

He never asked why I didn’t show up that day. And I never told him I’d been keeping my mother away from a bottle of expired pills.

He’ll never know my silence wasn’t rejection. It was fear. Guilt.

And a kind of love that wanted him to stay golden, even if I turned to ash.

I don’t remember the exact day it shifted.

It wasn’t thunder or some movie-worthy breakdown. It was quiet.

I’d wake up and stare at the ceiling for an hour. Not moving.

Not checking my phone.

Smiling when expected, nodding when spoken to, but inside, it was dark.

Like someone had turned off the lights and left me in an empty theater.

I stopped reading. Stopped praying.

Even the sky lost its colors. I told myself I was just tired.

But each day felt like wet clothes I couldn’t take off.

Then I dreamed I was falling, gently, like gravity was being kind.

No fear. Just relief.

When I woke up, I thought:

Maybe it’s time.

That was the day I searched how many sleeping pills it would take to never wake up.

I didn’t do it, not that day.

Mom was coughing in the next room.

She looked at me with hollow eyes and said, “You’re all I have left.”

And I froze.

But the thought stayed.

It kept coming back, softer, sweeter. Like a lullaby with teeth.

Ishan texted that week.

Hope you’re okay.

I stared at it, then turned my phone off. What could I say?

That I was imagining vanishing?

That I couldn’t bear my own reflection? No.

I loved him too much to hand him that weight.

Sometimes I’d watch birds cut across the dusk sky. I used to think I was one of them.

Now I felt like the sky itself, vast, empty, letting everyone else pass through.

I didn’t want to die.

I wanted the pain to stop.

The guilt. The exhaustion. The pretending.

I wanted someone to hold me and say,

“You don’t have to be strong anymore. I see you. All of you. And you don’t scare me.”

But no one did.

So maybe it was time to stop waiting.

That day, hope in me faded, quietly, like a candle that burns out while no one’s watching.

Chapter 14

The pages smelled like her.

That faint scent of old ink, sandalwood oil, and something I could only call Anya.

I was sitting in her room, now a museum of stillness, the fan rotating lazily above, her bedsheets untouched, her pillow holding the shape of a head that would never

return.

And in my lap: her diary.

The second one.

I had read the first. The poems, the trip memories, the laughter held tightly between aching lines.

But this one… this one was different.

I didn’t flip to the middle.

I didn’t start from the first page.

I opened where the bookmark had been left, torn from a notebook, with a half-finished doodle on it. Probably hers.

And then I read.

"Then came the dream. I was falling. Off a cliff. But gently. Like gravity was trying to be kind..."

My breath hitched. I kept reading.

Her words weren’t metaphors anymore. They were confessions.

Naked. Quiet. Final.

Her pain wasn’t just sadness, it was decay.

The kind you don’t even notice until you’re already buried beneath it.

I didn’t realize I was crying until a tear fell right on her sentence:

“I searched how many sleeping pills it would take to never wake up.”

My fingers froze on the page. My heart, gone.

I wanted to scream. Throw the book.

Punch a wall. Anything.

But all I could do was read.

Line after line of silent suffering she never showed me.

Moments I never noticed.

Smiles she forced when her soul was crumbling.

“I didn’t want to die. I wanted the pain to stop.” I bit my lip so hard it bled.

“I wanted someone to hold me and say, ‘You don’t have to be strong anymore. I see you. All of you. And you don’t scare me.’ But no one ever said that.”

My hands shook. Because I would’ve. God, I would’ve.

I would’ve stayed up all night.

I would’ve fought anyone, even her father, even fate, if she had just said something. Anything.

But she didn’t.

Because I was too busy “moving forward.”

Too busy trying to “let her go when she went silent.” I thought she needed space.

She needed saving.

And now… She was gone.

The one person who had seen me when I was invisible, the one who made my birthdays

meaningful and my jokes worth telling, had suffered in silence because I didn’t try hard enough.

She had written it all down. All of it.

Every ache.

And I found it too late.

I buried my face into the pages.

Like maybe if I held them tight enough, they’d become her voice again.

Maybe if I cried hard enough, she’d come back. Maybe this was a nightmare.

But it wasn’t.

It was her goodbye, hidden in ink.

And I was the fool who thought a “Hope you’re okay” text was enough to keep her breathing.

That’s when I saw the envelope, tucked behind the last page.

My name on it. Just one word:

"Ishan."

Her handwriting. And I knew…

This was her final letter.

Chapter 15

Dear Ishu,

I know you never liked when I called you that. You’d frown, pretend to be annoyed, and say,

“Stop it, Anya. Call me Ishan.”

But the truth? You loved it when I called you Ishu. I could see it in your eyes.

And now… I’m saying it one last time.

Because when you finish this letter, there will never be another “Ishu” from me. This will be the last time your Anya the Brave

ever speaks to you.

Only, I’m not brave anymore. Maybe I never was.

I pretended for years. I built this mask of laughter and “I’m fine” until even you, the one who saw through me the best, began to believe some parts of it. But Ishu… deep down, I’ve been breaking for a long time. And this time, I don’t think I can piece myself back together.

If you’re reading this, it means I’ve let go. It means I’ve chosen the quiet.

It means I’m not coming back.

I can already imagine the look in your eyes. I’ve replayed it so many times in my head that it hurts. I know you’ll be angry. You’ll be hurt. You’ll feel betrayed. And maybe you’ll hate me. And you have every right to.

But please… please read all of this before you decide how to remember me.

Ishu… it’s not that you didn’t matter. You did. You mattered more than the air in my lungs. You were the one thing in this world that felt safe, even when everything else was on fire. I am writing this only to you — not to my parents, not to anyone else, because you’re the only one who ever truly knew me.

Do you remember when we were in grade 8, and the bullying started? I told you I was fine. I lied. Every word they said stuck to me like shards of glass, cutting me every time I looked in the mirror. They made me feel small, ugly, worthless. And you, you would have fought the whole world for me if I told you. But I didn’t. Because I knew you would lose friends for me. And I couldn’t bear to make your world smaller because of my pain. But you found out and that problem got solved.

Then home stopped being home. Papa’s voice got sharper, Mumma’s eyes got dimmer. I could hear them breaking in the next room. I used to sit with

my back against my bedroom door at night, just to feel like I was holding the pieces together. I wasn’t. I couldn’t. And slowly, I stopped being able to hold myself together too.

But you… you stayed. You always stayed. Not just when I asked, but when I couldn’t. You saw things no one else noticed. The way my hands shook when I was scared. The way my smile never quite reached my eyes on bad days. You’d ask, quietly, “Are you okay?”

And I’d lie. Again. And you’d let me. But I saw the worry in your face. I saw the way you carried my pain even when I never asked you to.

That’s the thing, Ishu. You started carrying too much of me.

You had your dreams, those big, wild dreams that made your eyes light up when you talked about them. You had your plans, your life, your sky to fly in. And yet… you started staying grounded because you didn’t want to leave me behind.

And that was killing me inside.

Because I realized I wasn’t just drowning, I was pulling you under with me.

So I started pushing you away. Slowly, at first. Delayed replies. “Sorry, busy.” “Tired.” “Maybe next time.”

But inside, I was sitting on the floor of my room, hugging my knees, too exhausted to even cry.

You noticed. I know you did. But you didn’t leave. And maybe that’s why this hurts so much.

I still remember the last time we saw each other properly. You talked about the stars. You were laughing. And I thought, “God, how can someone carry so much light?” I wanted to tell you that I loved you. Not just as a friend. Not just as the boy who knew my soul. But as the only person I would have chosen in every version of my life. But I didn’t. Because I knew I was already fading.

Then came my birthday.

You called. You texted. You waited.

I saw it all. I read your “Happy birthday, Anya. Please come, just for an hour.” And I wanted to. I swear I wanted to. But Ishu, I didn’t have the courage. I didn’t have the money for the bus.

I didn’t have the strength to show up pretending I was okay.

I pictured your face when I walked in, and I knew I wouldn’t be able to fake the smile you deserved. So I stayed in bed. And hated myself for it.

I’ve kept everything you ever gave me.

That bracelet from grade 6? It’s still on my wrist. The paper boat from the rainy day? It’s still in my drawer.

Even the candy wrapper you folded into a heart, I have it tucked in the pages of my diary. You probably forgot about it, but I never did. Those little things… they were my lifelines.

On the worst nights, I’d take them out, hold them, and pretend I was still the girl who believed in tomorrows.

Ishu, I didn’t leave because I stopped loving you. I left because I loved you too much.

Too much to watch you crumble under the weight of my storms. Too much to let you keep trying to save me when I was already halfway gone.

When I’m gone, please, live. Don’t turn your life into a shrine for my memory. Don’t lock your heart. Don’t let my absence be the reason you stop loving this world. Go to those mountains you always talked about. Write your book. Laugh until your ribs hurt. Fall in love. Have a family. And maybe… maybe if you ever have a daughter, call her Anya. Tell her I was a girl who loved you so fiercely that she let go, so you could fly.

I’ll still be here in small ways. In the first rain of the season. In the smell of your old books. In the quiet moments when you feel someone watching over you.

I’m sorry. I’m sorry I wasn’t stronger. I’m sorry for every moment I made you worry. I’m sorry for the

goodbye I can’t say in person. But thank you, for being my home in a world that never felt safe.

I’ll love you in every lifetime. Even from far, far away.

Forever yours,

Anya the Brave

(who wasn’t brave enough… but loved you more than she ever said out loud)

The envelope was thin. Too light to matter.

But my hands shook like I was holding the weight of the universe.

Her handwriting was on the front, uneven, rushed, familiar.

"For Ishu."

I almost smiled when I saw it. Almost. But then my stomach twisted, because the last time she called me Ishu was… I couldn’t even remember.

I sat on my bed. No, I couldn’t. My legs carried me to the floor instead, my back pressed against the wall, the letter trembling between my fingers.

I tore it open.

And then, her voice. Not out loud, but in my head. Every word was her voice, the way she spoke when she was trying not to cry.

The first few lines hit like a soft wind. Then the next like a knife.

And then the rest… like a storm I couldn’t breathe in.

I read about the bullying, things she never told me. My chest tightened so hard it hurt to inhale. I read about her parents, and I remembered the nights she’d text me “I’m tired” and disappear. I read about the birthday. God, the birthday.

I had waited for hours that day, my phone glued to my palm. I’d told myself she was busy, she’d come later. I’d even saved a seat for her at the café. I sat there like an idiot, guarding it from strangers.

She never came. And now I knew why.

And it broke me in a way that felt final.

By the time I reached the part where she said she loved me too much to let me drown with her… I couldn’t see the paper anymore. My tears had blurred her words into water stains.

I pressed the letter to my face. It still smelled faintly of her, the same faint vanilla and rain she always carried.

It wasn’t enough. It wasn’t her.

I curled forward, my forehead touching the floor, the letter crumpled in my grip. My chest was heaving, but no sound came out at first. Just this silent, shaking grief that felt like it was tearing muscle from bone.

Then the sobs broke through. Loud, desperate, ugly. The kind of sound you make when you’ve lost something you’ll never get back.

Her words kept replaying in my head. Name your daughter Anya.

How the hell was I supposed to even think about having a daughter, when I couldn’t even survive this moment?

I wanted to scream at her. I wanted to hold her.

I wanted to tell her she was wrong, that I would have carried her storm, her weight, all of it. That I wouldn’t have drowned. That I would have kept her afloat even if it killed me.

But the truth was…

She wasn’t here to listen anymore.

The room felt too small, the air too thick. I stumbled to my desk, where the old paper boat sat — the one we made years ago. I picked it up, my tears

falling onto its edges, making the paper soft, fragile, like her.

And I broke again.

That night, I slept on the floor, clutching the letter and the paper boat like they were the last pieces of her I had left.

Because in some cruel way, they were.

And in the quiet, with my eyes burning and my heart refusing to slow down, I whispered into the darkness,

"I’ll always be your Ishu. Even if you’re not here to call me that anymore."

Morning.

I woke to sunlight sneaking through the half-drawn curtains. For a second, I forgot. For a second, I thought I’d hear her voice telling me to get up.

But the silence was absolute. And it hit me all over again.

The letter was still clutched in my fist, wrinkled from the night. My body ached from the floor, but I couldn’t bring myself to move. Not yet.

When I finally did, my eyes landed on something near the side of her bed, a small wooden box.

I pulled it toward me slowly, like it might shatter if I touched it wrong. I lifted the lid.

Inside was her life in pieces.

The bracelet I gave her in grade 6, faded but still whole.

The paper boat we made that rainy day, its edges soft from age but still holding its shape.

The candy wrapper I folded into a heart. She had kept it.

Old letters I’d written her silly notes from class, birthday wishes, random thoughts. Every single one was there, folded neatly, as if she’d been guarding them.

My throat tightened so much I could barely breathe.

Underneath it all, I found something else , my old hoodie. The one I gave her years ago when she was shivering at the bus stop. I thought she’d forgotten about it. She hadn’t. It still smelled faintly of her shampoo, and I pressed it to my face, my tears soaking into the fabric.

And then… at the very bottom… a photograph.

It was us. Sitting by the lake, the sunlight in her hair. She wasn’t looking at the camera, she was laughing at something I said. I wasn’t looking at the camera either. I was looking at her.

I pressed the photo to my chest, my whole body shaking.

I don’t know how long I sat there. Minutes. Hours. Time stopped meaning anything. I just kept tracing her handwriting on the folded notes, touching the things she touched, as if they could bridge the impossible gap between us.

At some point, her mother knocked softly and left a glass of water by the door. She didn’t say anything. She didn’t need to.

When I finally stood, I didn’t put the box back. I hugged it to my chest like it was her. Like if I let go, she’d vanish completely.

I walked to her window and looked outside, the same view she must have seen a thousand times. The street, the sky, the world that had gone on without her.

And I whispered into the still air,

"I’m still your Ishu. Always. Even if you’re not here to call me that anymore."

Chapter 16

I don’t know how long I’d been sitting there, staring at the same

patch of floor, the world around me nothing more than a blur of silence. My fingers were numb, my eyes dry and sore from the hours, maybe days, of crying. Then my gaze landed on the edge of her photo frame, peeking out from under a stack of papers on the table. I

reached for it without thinking.

It was the photo from that trip years ago, the one where she had that stubborn little smile,

the one that told you she knew life wasn’t easy but she’d stand against it anyway. I traced the curve of her cheek with my thumb, almost expecting the warmth of her skin to seep through. But it was just cold glass.

And then it hit me, the weight of it, she would never take another photo. That smile was now frozen in time, and all the dreams she carried… they were stranded too, unless someone picked them up.

For the first time since she left, I felt something different. Not less pain, no, the pain was still there, sharp and deep, but a flicker of… purpose.

I remembered the nights we stayed up talking about the book we’d write. How she said words

could outlive people, how she wanted to publish something that mattered. I remembered the tiny dreams she’d collect like seashells, learning to bake a perfect cake, watching the sunrise from a mountaintop, holding her own book in her hands.

All of it felt unfinished. And if I stopped here, if I let myself fade with her, then it would all stay unfinished.

“No,” I murmured, voice breaking. “No, I’m not letting it end like this.”

I didn’t even realize I was speaking to her photo until I saw my own reflection in the glass, red-eyed and hollow but… alive.

“I’ll finish the book, Anya. I’ll chase every dream you didn’t get to. And one day, when it’s out there in the world, I’ll know you’re somewhere, smiling at me like you did that day.”

The tears came again, but this time they weren’t only from loss, they were from the terrifying, fragile knowledge that I had something to live for. I kept holding her photo for a long time, afraid that if I set it down, that flicker of purpose might disappear. My hands felt heavy, but my chest… lighter, in a strange way. I ran my thumb over the edge of the frame once more before placing it carefully on my desk, right beside the open notebook that had been gathering dust for months.

The pen lay where I had abandoned it last, a single unfinished sentence staring back at me, mocking me with its incompleteness. For weeks, maybe longer, I hadn’t been able to write. Every time I tried, the words felt hollow, meaningless.

But now… now the silence felt different.

I pulled the chair closer and sat down. My hands shook as I picked up the pen, not from fear this time, but from the weight of knowing this mattered. The story wasn’t just mine anymore. It was hers. Ours.

The first line I wrote was clumsy, but I didn’t stop to fix it. I wrote another, and another. The pen scratched against the paper, the ink bleeding into the page like it had been waiting all this time.

Somewhere in the back of my mind, I could hear her voice, teasing, encouraging, sometimes laughing at my awful metaphors. I could almost imagine her leaning over my shoulder, reading the words as I wrote them.

And for the first time in forever, I didn’t feel like I was writing into an empty world.

I was writing to her.

I knew it wouldn’t be easy, chasing down all those dreams, bringing them to life, but I had made a promise. And I wasn’t going to break it. Not to her. Not to myself.

When I finally put the pen down, I realized hours had passed. The pages were filled. My tea had gone cold. And her photo was still watching over me from the corner of the desk, her smile unchanged.

Only now, I felt like I understood it.

That night, I didn’t fall asleep right away. I just sat there, my head resting on folded arms, staring at her photo until my eyes blurred. The ache was still there, deep and unshakable, but now it lived beside something else, something warmer.

It was strange… the pain didn’t vanish, but it no longer felt like it was pulling me under. It felt like a reminder, a sharp edge keeping me awake, alive, pushing me forward.

Somewhere between the grief and the promise I’d made, I realized this was not an ending. Not for her, and not for me.

Maybe my life had been shattered, but now I had the pieces. And piece by piece, I would build something she would be proud of.

I whispered one last time into the quiet room, “For you, Anya.”

And in the stillness, I almost believed I heard her whisper back.

Chapter 17

Time, I realized, doesn’t heal everything. It changes us. It carries

sorrow into the quiet corners of our days and teaches us how to live with it. But I never forgot her, never a single day. Anya was with me in the ink of every page I wrote, in every whispered hope, in the smallest of decisions. She had shaped the man I had

become.

I still remember the mornings she would wake before the sun, the way her hair fell across her face when she was lost in a book, the soft sound of her laughter when I made a terrible joke. Every memory replayed in my mind as I sat at my desk, holding the first printed copy of the book we had dreamed about together. Every word was a memory, every sentence a conversation frozen in time. Sometimes, late at night, I would read passages aloud, imagining her gleaming eyes watching me, smiling at the sentences we had once discussed. Holding the book in my hands, I felt her there, not as a ghost, but as the quiet, persistent fire that had

always guided me.

Life moved forward, slowly, carefully. Love returned to me, softly, unexpectedly. I married, and the day our daughter was born, I stared down at her tiny, delicate face, her fingers curling around mine, and the world felt infinite and fragile all at once. I knew her name immediately. Anya. My little Anya. The living embodiment of the girl who had taught me how to endure, to dream, and to live fully despite loss.

Watching her grow brought a flood of memories, her laughter echoing through our home, her small triumphs and stumbles, the spark of curiosity in her eyes. Each time she smiled, I felt the Anya I had loved all over again, her courage and joy flowing into the next generation. I remembered her insistence on capturing every small moment, her love for tiny victories and quiet sunsets. And I realized that this was the ultimate fulfillment of her dream: to be remembered not just in stories, but in life itself.

And my writing… our writing… it became more than words on paper. I published the book we had begun together, dedicating it to her. I included lines she had once whispered to me, her favorite metaphors, her secret jokes hidden between sentences. Every review, every message from someone touched by the words reminded me that she was still shaping the world, even after she had

gone. I named my successes after her, every small achievement a tribute to the girl who had shown me how to keep dreaming.

In quiet moments, when the house was still and my daughter slept, I would look at her photo on my desk, the same one I had held on that fateful night, and whisper, “This is for you, Anya. For every dream you carried, for every story we shared, for every life you still touch.”

And in that silence, I felt it: peace. Not the absence of sorrow, but the presence of love, memory, and purpose. Anya had never truly left me. She had become a part of everything I was, everything I did, and everything I would ever be.

She lived in my words, in my family, in the life I had built. I saw her in the first steps of my daughter, in the pages of our book that reached strangers across the world, in every sunrise I watched with a quiet smile. And finally, after all the grief, all the sleepless nights, all the empty mornings, I understood. The best way to honor her wasn’t to hold onto the past, it was to live the life she had inspired me to live, fully, fearlessly, and with every ounce of love I had left to give.

And so I lived, for her, through her, and with her in every heartbeat.

Epilogue

Even now, I find myself searching for her in the smallest places.

A breeze that feels too familiar.

A song that sounds like something she would hum under her breath.

The quiet way the night holds me when I’m alone. She isn’t here, yet she is everywhere. I used to believe tomorrow was just another day, a blank space waiting to be filled. But now I know tomorrow carries her. Not her face, not her voice, but the weight of her absence, the echo of her laughter, the warmth of her memory.

I thought I lost her the day she left this world, but the truth is, I carry her in every decision, every word, every fragile hope I allow myself to hold. She is not gone; she has simply changed her place. She lives in my grief, in my pages, in my quiet victories.

Anya exists in my every tomorrow. Not as a shadow of what was, but as a promise of what will always be.

And now, I step in, not as Ishan, not as Anya, but as the one who wrote them into being.

To you, Ishan: your voice has carried this story, but your silence carried the weight. You searched for her in the world and found her in yourself. You loved her in ways you could never say, and now your life is proof that love does not end with loss. It bends, reshapes, but never ends.

To you, Anya: though paper holds your voice and ink holds your pain, you are more than the sadness that closed your story. You are laughter that still lingers, bravery that was misunderstood, love that will outlast even these words. You exist in him, in me, and now in everyone who turned these pages.

And to you, the reader: this was never just a story. It was a memory disguised as fiction, a wound disguised as words. “You exist in my every tomorrow” is not only for Anya—it is for everyone we have loved and lost, everyone whose absence reshaped us.

If you’ve reached this last page and felt her presence, even for a moment, then she has lived again. And maybe that’s enough.

She exists. In Ishan. In me. And now,

in you.
